We set out in the morning, warily checking windows, corners, anywhere the Germans could spring a trap or an ambush. 

Johannson was in the lead, Garand at the ready and bayonet fixed improperly. Rook was shadowing him, double checking each spot that Johannson had checked before. I was in the middle with Peters and his trusty sniper rifle, carrying the M2 Browning. And Stewart was in the rear, covering our backs with his Thompson at the ready.

The others had been glancing uncertainly at the MG I held in my hands, but I quickly dismissed the growing fear as they were undoubtly only nervous about a rookie with such a powerful weapon.

It was quiet. Too quiet.

The bridge we had set out to capture was undefended, and we quickly set up a defensive position in case a German patrol stumbled upon us.

The sound started as a low rumble. We looked around, at each other, confused as to why the ground was shaking. It got louder, and we could soon hear the sound of people yelling. We readied our weapons, getting ready for the enemy to throw a grenade or fire a Panzerschreck.

But nothing could prepare us for what happened next.

A giant tide of German soldiers, all carrying trench shovels and primed Steilhandgranates in their hands, came around the corner, rushing at us screaming at the top of their lungs.

We opened fire, but there were too many and we were quickly overrun.

Stewart was the first to go, having gotten overzealous with his Thompson. He had managed to push the wave of Germans back, when they surrounded him and began pummeling him to death with their shovels. 

One of them, holding a grenade, charged Rook and Johannson from behind. They never saw it coming.

By now, it was only me and Peters, him firing his sniper rifle with reckless abandon.  Running out of ammo, Peters quickly pulled out his M1911 and managed to squeeze off a few shots, but it wasn't long before he too was buried under the mass of grey and black.

I was cornered, MG propped up against an overturned cart while I mowed down soldier after soldier, spent casings flying everywhere.  From out of nowhere, a fist collided with my face and I blacked out.

Waking up, I found I was tied down to a chair in a pitch black room.  The only thing visible was a glowing box directly in front of me with words written on it.  Squinting my eyes, I barely made out the small, black letters.

The box read:

[b]Kicked from server.  Reason: lol dont use MG skrub [/b]

Day of Defeat (DoD) is a solid old skool squad Shooter that is probably on its way out at no fault of its own. It is still semi-active and has a fairly strong community of dedicated long time players. There is also bots and they are good. I feel bad for putting this game one on the way side. Placed in exchange for more modern shooters emerging at the time. Mainly leaving for online competitive leader boards. Day of Defeat was a very competitive shooter in its time and it still holds it titles up today. You don't lose your championship belt when you retire. No different than what R6 or CS is today. We aim trained, we practiced, we farmed. It was the start of what became hardcore titles. I remember back in 2020 a group of friends and I where playing.  Many games were getting remade around this time and the hard core genre was being defined. We talked about why DoD was not getting any meaningful updates or even a full remake, like the other games of the time. The conclusion we came to was that Day of Defeat does not need a remake. "Don't fix what aint broke" There is nothing wrong with this classic shooter, not even today. So do your self a favor. Put down the competitive shooter of 2025 and have some fun instead. Todays shooter will be as dead as Day of Defeat in ten years anyway. Take a moment to enjoy what you have while its there. Because before you know it, the fun has passed while you were too busy taking things seriously and you end up missing all the actual fun to be had. Please don't make the same mistake I did. Play the games you love to play, not just what everyone else is playing. Because eventually there will be no more players and no more servers for the game you actually enjoy. Instead you wasted that chance trying to force your self to stay in the competitive zone. Grab some buds and a couple copies of the game on sale. "This is where the fun begins!" To the guys who stayed with Day of Defeat I say this: You hold Solace in knowing you made the right choice. I commend you for your dedication. "hold the line."

I never grew up playing this game, this is actually one of the few Valve games I have never played before. The other ones being Ricochet, Team Fortress classic and Deathmatch classic. I decided I'd try it out and it ain't half bad.

It feels like a mix between Counter Strike and Team Fortress. It's class-based like TF, but the gameplay is definitely a lot more like CS than TF. You die very quickly, usually in 1-2 shots and the gameplay revolves around sightlines and flanking rather than running in guns blazing.  It's not as strict as CS though as there's respawning and you can just choose whatever loadout you want before you start without needing to buy anything. 
The maps have lots of different ways to flank or surprise your enemy, usually there's buildings and side areas you can sneak around in to get the drop on someone. The guns are pinpoint accurate as long as you're standing still so it's a good idea to find yourself a good piece of cover and wait for the enemy to make the first move.

I don't have too much else to say about it other than if you don't enjoy that style of gameplay that something like CS has you probably won't like this either. The game does still have a dedicated following and I didn't have an issue finding a server even at 4am when I decided to try it out for the first time. I enjoyed it though, it's simple but fun enough.

Even though this game is not looking up to date, the base gameplay could feel flat and some mechanics are annoying to play with, but the overall game is challenging and still (surprisingly) playable in multiplayer. This is a simplified multiplayer team shooter, with class system. There is no perks, item drops at the end or cool weapon skins, and because of this the game could be a "fresh air to feel", comparing to the games nowadays.

It can be difficult to get used to the game, I think if you can get this one less than 0.5€ and don't mind it's age and get some friends to play with you (just in case), you can still have decent fun with this one.

Enlist in an intense brand of Axis vs. Allied teamplay set in the WWII European Theatre of Operations. Players assume the role of light/assault/heavy infantry, sniper or machine-gunner class, each with a unique arsenal of historical weaponry at their disposal. Missions are based on key historical operations. And, as war rages, players must work together with their squad to accomplish a variety of mission-specific objectives.

Day of Defeat, ladies and gentlemen, it's quite something, really tremendous. It's got that World War II vibe, very classy, very historical. The atmosphere, my friends, it's like you're right there in the middle of the action. And let me be clear, the gameplay is fantastic, believe me. Maybe not the best graphics, but who needs that when you've got the best gameplay, folks? It's an exceptional video game that captures the essence of World War II in an impressive way. The attention to detail and historical accuracy is truly commendable. This game fosters a sense of teamwork and camaraderie that reflects the values of unity and working together. I highly recommend 'Day of Defeat' for those who appreciate history and enjoy first-person shooters.

Graphics are dated, gameplay is simple, the learning curve can be punishing for new (also to CS) players, servers are few and the player base is small. Among the servers that still run, some have great vanilla and modded maps with often interesting adjustments. There's a class/gun and playing style for everyone, regardless of skill or playing background. When there are only a few players on a map, it feels like a duel where the stakes are high and where you alone can turn the tide and when it's full, it feels like a proper skirmish, where everyone contributes their piece but where the group is more important than the individual. Both have their distinct charms. Personally, I find the bot servers  ( players only vs bots only) more enjoyable - though I'm very decent in PvP - because they're the closest thing to ideal co-op gameplay in a FPS landscape where everyone's out for themselves. Instead, tactics matter, communication is king, support is reassuringly given and returned, and you truly feel like a team.

Again, the game may be old...
...but newer is not always better.

📜 Overview
Day of Defeat (DoD) is a team-based multiplayer first-person shooter developed by Valve. Initially released as a mod for Half-Life in 2003, it was later re-released as a standalone game in 2005. The game is set during World War II, and players are divided into two teams: the Axis and the Allies. The gameplay centers around capturing objectives, strategic teamwork, and tactical combat in a variety of historically-inspired maps. Day of Defeat offers a realistic yet fast-paced experience that blends historical accuracy with arcade-style action.

🌟 Pros
✅ Tactical Team Play – The game emphasizes teamwork, with each class having its strengths, such as medics, riflemen, and engineers.
✅ Historical Maps – The environments are inspired by real WWII battles, offering a unique and immersive atmosphere.
✅ Varied Classes and Roles – Different character classes provide diverse playstyles, allowing players to experiment with tactics.
✅ Addictive Gameplay – The combination of objectives-based missions and high-stakes combat keeps players engaged.

Released in 2003 by Valve, Day of Defeat is a multiplayer first-person shooter set in the European theater of World War II. Players can choose to fight for either the Allied or Axis forces, with gameplay built heavily around teamwork and strategy. The game does a solid job of immersing players in the WWII setting. From the weapons and uniforms to the level design, the attention to detail helps sell the historical theme and makes battles feel grounded in the era. Matches are entirely team-focused, with players needing to work closely together to succeed. Whether you’re defending objectives or pushing forward, coordination with your squad is essential. Lone-wolf play doesn’t get you far here. Both factions come equipped with a wide range of period-accurate weapons. Each option feels distinct and offers different tactical advantages, giving players the chance to experiment with various playstyles. The maps cover a variety of battlefields, from narrow city streets and quiet villages to forested areas and open warzones. This variety forces you to adapt your strategies depending on the environment, which keeps the gameplay fresh. One of the game’s strongest aspects is its modding and community-driven content. Players have created new maps, mods, and features over the years, which has helped keep the experience alive long after release. Even decades later, Day of Defeat still has an active fan base. Its replayability and community support have given it impressive staying power compared to many other shooters from the same era. For anyone who enjoys team-based shooters with a historical backdrop, Day of Defeat is a classic worth revisiting. Its combination of atmosphere, strategic depth, and community support makes it stand out, even today.

As said, Day of Defeat is a WW2 shooter. Team and class based. A mix between arcade and realism. Weapons are as deadly as in many such shooters, just having single person rush forward will do no good, should do that in team. Many weapons also have big recoil, which depends on your stance: moving, standing, crouching or prone. Yes, camping is a viable strategy here, but I feel that I have more chance to break through camping than in, say, Counter-strike. Players can respawn any time, so putting yourself to risk isn't bad idea. Each character also have a stamina, which is used when you spring and jump, slowly recovering afterwards. The slowing effect after using it is quite punishing, so you should sprint from cover to cover. Don't use sprint when moving to the front from the spawn point.
Maps are designed to be more of pipes, like classic maps, not open fields, providing a main path and few flanking routes. Even more curious, the maps are assymetrical, which may possibly provide some inbalance (I think that Nazis in Avalanche map have height advantage). Breaks the usual symmetry monotony though, more interesting. Some maps even feature British forces instead of American ones. (they have less classes though)

Day of Defeat, developed and published by Valve, stands as one of the defining multiplayer shooters of the early 2000s, a title that carved its identity through tactical, class-based combat rooted in the grim backdrop of World War II. Originally born as a Half-Life mod before evolving into a full standalone release, the game epitomizes the era when teamwork, precision, and map control mattered more than flashy effects or cinematic flair. Released in 2003, it quickly distinguished itself from its contemporaries by prioritizing realistic combat flow, deliberate pacing, and objective-driven matches that rewarded communication and strategic positioning. Where many shooters of the time leaned toward chaos, Day of Defeat thrived on order—the kind built through discipline, coordination, and an understanding of battlefield roles.

The game’s premise is straightforward yet highly effective. Players join either the Allied or Axis side and select from a range of classes—riflemen, machine gunners, snipers, support gunners, and more—each offering distinct weapons and abilities. These roles force you to think beyond yourself, to work in tandem with your squad to capture points or plant explosives across compact but thoughtfully designed maps. The map design remains one of the game’s strongest achievements. Every street, alley, and bunker feels purposeful, crafted to create tension and encourage cooperation. Instead of sprawling open battlefields, Day of Defeat thrives in the confines of narrow, war-torn environments that force constant interaction. You’re always in motion—flanking, defending, or supporting—never wandering aimlessly. The intensity of the encounters gives each victory, no matter how small, a real sense of earned accomplishment.

Mechanically, Day of Defeat walks a fine line between accessibility and realism. The GoldSrc engine, the same technology behind Half-Life and Counter-Strike, gives the game a weighty, tactile feel. Weapons have punch and recoil; shooting on the move affects accuracy; suppression from machine-gun fire can keep entire teams pinned down. It’s a design that rewards patience and punishes recklessness. Unlike run-and-gun shooters, you can’t rely on twitch reflexes alone—timing your reloads, learning the recoil patterns, and positioning yourself smartly often make the difference between life and death. The sound design complements this perfectly: bullets snap through the air, grenades crack with echoing force, and distant gunfire tells you exactly where the front line is shifting. Even today, these small touches give the game a level of immersion that outlasts its dated visuals.

Visually, Day of Defeat clearly reflects its time, with low-resolution textures, simple models, and modest lighting effects. Yet there’s an understated beauty in its design philosophy. The muted tones and dilapidated architecture create a convincing sense of place, capturing the desolation of European towns ravaged by war. The minimalist interface keeps attention squarely on the action, and the absence of unnecessary clutter or modern HUD elements makes each engagement feel raw and immediate. The game’s age actually works to its advantage—it strips away distractions, allowing players to focus entirely on movement, teamwork, and survival. It’s a product of an era where polish came from gameplay balance rather than graphical fidelity, and Day of Defeat remains a testament to that philosophy.

As a multiplayer experience, the game’s staying power comes from its reliance on cooperation rather than individual dominance. No single player can win a match alone; the objectives demand coordination, with each class contributing to a shared effort. Communication, whether through voice chat or quick commands, becomes essential. Matches can feel chaotic at first, but as players fall into rhythm—riflemen covering chokepoints, machine gunners setting up suppressive fire, snipers locking down sightlines—the game transforms into a deeply satisfying dance of strategy and precision. It’s a system that rewards mutual understanding rather than ego, and that makes each victory genuinely collective.

Over time, Day of Defeat has understandably aged, especially compared to modern shooters with sprawling maps, progression systems, and cinematic flair. Yet its core appeal remains timeless. It represents a purer form of multiplayer design—tight, focused, and built on mechanics rather than spectacle. Its influence can be felt in later tactical shooters that prioritize teamwork over chaos, and it continues to attract a dedicated community that values its straightforward yet demanding gameplay. For new players, it may lack the gloss of modern titles, but for veterans and enthusiasts of classic design, it offers a reminder of what made early online shooters so compelling. Day of Defeat is not just a nostalgic relic; it’s a benchmark of precision, teamwork, and the kind of balance that many modern games still strive to achieve.

This is a WWII multiplayer shooter that was originally created as a Half-Life mod, and was given a standalone release as one of Steam's very first games. That alone gives it some trivia value, and I'd say it's a nice old-school game on its own merits too.

The game's default maps are set in the Western European portion of the war, and it has more of them than its sequel [url=http://steamcommunity.com/id/trar/recommended/300]Day of Defeat: Source[/url] has out of the box. Most notably, unlike the sequel, some of them feature the British as the Allied faction while a couple maps are paratrooper missions where one side deploys from landed gliders. It's still fun to play, despite showing its age and being kinda janky from attempting tactical combat with the original HL engine. It's rawer than DoD: Source with punchy, crunchy weapon sounds, and definitely rawer than your average modern multiplayer shooter. Its gameplay is an interesting fast-paced tactical-arcade mix with high recoil and no frills, straight out of the early 2000s and pretty refreshing compared to more modern shooters. You could roughly sum it up as a class-based [url=http://steamcommunity.com/id/trar/recommended/10]Counter-Strike[/url] equivalent with respawning, one that encourages a little more teamwork than CS does.

I would definitely recommend picking this up for 50 cents (or your local equivalent) during a sale and trying it out if you're into WWII and/or old-school shooters - not much to lose if you don't like it, after all. It isn't dead, I thought it would be, but it wasn't and there are still many many servers to choose. I would advise [FULL METAL JACKET]  for a server to play on with a range of maps and there are always players playing. 
For the price of three pounds ninety-nine pence, no that isn't American currency - I can't be arsed - it is a great shooter and more than worth every penny.
Also, like me, if your internet isn't very good, download "Sturmbot" for free, where you can play on virtually any map with really intelligent bots offline, probably the best bots/AI player mod for any game I've ever played. This also enables you to play on a full sever even just on your own or with a small group of friends - it's great.

One of the finest examples of "Old is Gold". The original Day of Defeat is simple and doesn't try to do anything out of the ordinary. It's easy to get into and the rules of the game are simple. You can capture all the flags to win the round or destroy objectives. Each faction (there are 3 in total, British, American and German but mostly the latter 2) has unique classes with different weapons. None of which are overpowered and thus no one really gravitates toward any single one.

Furthermore, there are custom maps made by the players themselves, paving the way for some truly unique maps and gameplay. These maps are hosted on community run servers. You can pick a classic server where you go head to head with one another, or go for the Humans vs Bots servers, Either way, you're gonna be in for quite a fun time in Day of Defeat.

A true classic. A very outstanding title in the gaming industry.
The game takes place during World War II, where two sides (Axis and Allies) are fighting eachother. Both sides have 9 different classes, which are almost identical in each pair. The maps are great. Most of them have simple flag capture points, but one can even try the Normandy landings for example, where the Axis defend and the Allies attack. I have to say that it feels really good to open fire on the landing Allies.
In summary the gameplay is simple and enjoyable. The game still has a small community: one server is often close to full. The only problem with this game is its age. Control and movement are difficult to master.
This game is really worth trying. I'm sure it won't be your favorite, but it can certainly provide a good experience for a few hours.

There is something strangely attractive about GoldSrc games. Sure, if you're in a wrong mood it could feel even borderline depressive, but if you feel ok and have some free time to dive into - let's face it - pretty much not alive game in terms of player-base, you can get an interesting experience.
It's like Team Fortress in the setting of World War 2 - fast respawns (a.k.a. no time wasting like in Counter Strike), point captures, classes.

Plus, i think WW2 is much more interesting setting than any modern warfare type of game. Or even any historical setting.

Hey Valve, how about a sequel?..
